blogs.title: The "Update" Loophole: How Terse Declarations Sustain FOIA Withholdings Over Time
blogs.description: This post analyzes the D.C. Circuit's approach to the 'pending or reasonably anticipated' requirement of FOIA Exemption 7(A). Specifically, it examines the court's reasoning in Farahi v. FBI, where it held that a terse, conclusory 'update' declaration could be sufficient to sustain a withholding if it merely confirms earlier, more detailed evidence. The post will discuss the implications for practitioners on how to challenge 'stale' government declarations and whether this lowers the evidentiary bar for agencies to maintain long-term secrecy over ongoing investigations.

blogs.title: Shadow Litigation: The Role of Ex Parte Declarations in FOIA Enforcement
blogs.description: This post explores the procedural tension between the transparency goals of FOIA and the government's use of ex parte, under-seal declarations to justify withholdings. By analyzing the court's admission that ex parte evidence 'handicaps' plaintiffs, the post discusses the inherent difficulty of challenging agency claims of national security or law enforcement interference when the evidence is shielded from the requester. It considers whether the current judicial approach provides sufficient oversight or effectively grants agencies a 'blank check' in counterterrorism contexts.

blogs.title: Information vs. Words: Parsing the "Inextricably Intertwined" Standard
blogs.description: This post focuses on the court's analysis of segregability under FOIA. It delves into the distinction the court draws between 'meaningful information' and 'individual words or phrases' that may be non-exempt but are not 'reasonably segregable.' The post will analyze the 'inextricably intertwined' doctrine and discuss the practical reality for plaintiffs seeking records from massive agency files (like Farahi's 10,000+ page file), where the government can claim that no single page is free of exempt material.
